editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: My name is William Grant Coleman, C-0-L-E-M-A-N.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Now, you were old enough to remember what the start of World War II was like in America. Can you tell us about Pearl Harbor day and how you heard about it and how you felt about it?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Well, the day that Pearl Harbor happened, I rode to school. At that time I was going to high school at Battise, Oklahoma, and I was in the tenth grade, the day Pearl Harbor started. And it was -- that was a surprise to me, as it was to most of America, I think. Had the Germans invaded, it would not have been a surprise because we had been hearing about them since 1939 in our -- by papers and, you know, radio, whatever and knew there was a lot of turmoil. And everyone was a little bit on edge. We was hoping the war wouldn't start. My folks were, of course. And I was -- at 13 years old at the time in'39, I wasn't thinking too much about it. With a little bit of dread but not a great deal. I had -- unlike anybody, I had a good pastoral, easy life. Hard work. But as far as being stressed out, I wasn't. To me, this big change in world events was kind of scary, yeah. It really was. Then when Pearl Harbor took place, December 7th, well, that was a real surprise, because we hadn't I had not had any indication in my in my life or my knowledge that the Japanese were would invade us. To me, it was ridiculous to think about. They found out it was, too, of course, you know, later on but after all they had attempted, hey, they couldn't pass that up. And I don't blame them, you know. It would be like bankers putting a load of money out on the street and say don't you rob me. {Laughter}. After all, you know -- so, as we found out since.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Do you remember on Monday when President Roosevelt spoke to Congress and the radio broadcast that speech? Did you get a chance to hear that speech?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: I did not. But the principal read it to us in assembly in the school about the -- the day of infamy, et cetera. And I've heard it many times since, of course. It was very serious. And we were all moved, of course, and to tell you the truth, unnerved by it. Very much so, because it changed people's lives. And did it change our lives. We all knew it. There wasn't a kid there that didn't know anything -- or a person. Yeah, we knew it.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What's your opinion of FDR?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: I think FDR would roll over in his grave if he knew what he had started, down the road to socialistic bologna. At the time I was growing up if you didn't work, you didn't eat. And that's all changed now. If you work, then you pay for somebody else to eat all the time that don't work. And he started it. And I'm not in favor of that. I'm a conservative. I have to say so, even though I draw compensation. But I earned it.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Now, down the road during the war there, we had rationing and all of those other things. How did your life in Oklahoma change with the war going on?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Well, I lived on a cattle ranch at that time, and I grew up on a cattle ranch. And about the only difference it made to us was sugar was a premium. And we didn't go to town often anyway. That didn't make a difference. But as far as that goes, all my dad did was he had a little pickup truck, he sold it. And that was the end of that until the war was over. We didn't -- he didn't use it. If he wanted to go to town or -- there was a bus occasionally. Because we lived in a very rural area. Highway 21 runs up through eastern Oklahoma through McCurtain County. And it's almost hard to -- it's hard to explain because it was a gravel state highway, but it was gravel. It wasn't even paved. And it run from 10 to 15 miles from the Arkansas line to the east. And we ran -- and the highway run north and south. And my dad leased bureau -- either Bureau of Land Management or from -- well, and there wasn't any warehouse then. But I think it's Choctaw Lumber Company. And Derricks was they owned all the land, the Choctaw Indian Nation. And Derricks managed it for them. My dad leased land for them to graze on, the cattle. We really didn't -- so the rationing didn't bother us all that much, to tell you the truth.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Great. So eventually you get drafted and wind up in the service. Tell us about that.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Well, see, I did not like -- I might have given the impression that I liked being -- I liked -- I didn't want to live -- be a see, a cowboy's life is not what Roy Rogers says it is. It's hard, tough. Broke. Work every day, seven-day-a-week. Cows don't have any schedule. It's a hard life. I wanted out of it. So I went to New Orleans when I got out of high school and cruised around a little bit and went to Houston, Texas. And that's where I got drafted when I become 18. I got out of high school in May for about three months. I went to Houston, Texas and that's when I got drafted there. Tried to get in the Navy, and it was too late. I couldn't volunteer for anything because they needed soldiers. I was class 1-A and that was it. But -- and that was the start of my military career. Yes, it was.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell us a little bit about training and take us all the way, you get to Europe. Wl:LLIAM GRANT COLEMAN: Well, I went through training at Fort Hood, Texas at that time, infantry training. And then my outfit was scheduled to go to the South Pacific. And having been a student of geography in my life, and I knew -- I didn't want any part of the South Pacific. Even though it looks like paradise, it is absolute green Hell. And I knew it. Malaria, bugs, heat, whatever. I thought whoa, I don't want to go there. And to try to find somebody, besides I don't want malaria, whatever. And I got a chance to join and volunteer for the Paratroopers. So I -- that's what I did. I volunteered for -- and I went to parachute school at Fort Benning,and then I went from Fort Benning to Europe with the Paratroopers.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell us about Paratrooper school in a couple of sentences; how would you describe it?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Parachute school was the nearest thing to taking a person to their absolute limits of endurance that you could possibly imagine. Now it would be considered torture. Every time a guy looked at you wrong, you did 50 pushups. We did -- we jogged from five to ten mile -- we did, yeah, ten miles, not kilometers, before breakfast every day. Every day. Seven days a week. The only thing good about the Paratroopers that I could see to have fun was jumping out of the planes. That was fun, because it didn't take much effort to get out of a plane. But everything else was effort, if you really want to know the truth. It was -- it was oh, man, if you were in good shape when you went to parachute school, you weren't in better shape. It tore you down. Actually I was in better shape when I went there out of the boot camp in the Army than I was when I left there, because I was absolutely exhausted when I left there. And that's the truth. Of course they hype you full of bologna that boy, you can take on the world and all this stuff. But that's strictly psychology. But everybody buys it. If you're only 18, 19 years old, of course you do. But that's -- but I liked the Airborne actually once I got out. First of all, I liked the 50 bucks a month more money for jump pay. Collect that.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: And you liked the glass boots and pick up -- better pick up more girls that way with glass boots.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Well, that's true. But in Columbus, Georgia where there was probably 5,000 women and 100,000 guys, that was kind of tough. That not -- but that's about the ratio, twenty to one of men and women. Available women anyway. My God. Of course, that was a -- every service camp at that time was the same way. And of course, that's all guys had on their minds was girls, of course. But Atlanta, that's a different story. Absolutely.Georgia was a nice state to get a little free time in. No doubt about it. I enjoyed it very much.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Why don't you tell us about the trip to Europe, how that was done and tell us a little bit about what it was like for you.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Well, we didn't fly over. We knew we were going in as replacement. Bastogne, we had -- the lOlst Paratroopers Airborne has jumped at Bastogne. And some of them went in gliders and some of them went in whatever. But they had taken Bastogne at the time that I was supposed to go in as a replacement. And instead of going in through Bastogne, I went on to Charleroi and then on up to Namur. And we kept following our outfit, and they kept moving. And then I went off jump status. I broke -- or fractured an ankle and went off jump status. They put me in the armored division, Fourth Armored Division, and we were -- as a replacement. But I didn't -- I never -- I never saw any action. The day that the war was over in Europe, well, they say it's in May, May 2nd or whatever. It was actually April the 15th we were on the border -- Chech border at Hoff, Germany waiting for the Russians. And when they came with their tanks and whatever, we left. And of course, our general and everybody there were really angry because we had been there a week. Hell, we could have gone on to Poland. But no way, the dye had been cast. We had given away east Europe. But none of us knew that at the time. Of course, history tells you that now, but we didn't know it then. We didn't even know what was going on. Why are we waiting for the Russians? Hey, what have they done? You know, well...

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Do you see any Russians? What was your general opinion/impression?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Dirty, ugly, stupid. Two-thirds of them were women in the tanks. The m€n and the women were -- talk about equality, that's right. And very, very -- they were not -- first of all, they had no class at all. That was my first opinion of the Russians, was silver teeth, always smiling and always saying I-know-something-you-don't-know look in their face and very, very almost animalistica lly dumb. Ridiculous. And it was a turn-off. Just the vibes turned me off. I didn't like them. I really didn't like them at all. First of all, I was mad because we couldn't keep going, you know, as, of course, was Patton. He was -- he was a soldier, not a politician, wasn't he?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: True. Well W ILLIAM GRANT COLEMAN: And that's about it. And then I spent a year -- a little over a year -- the war was over, and what I did was I extended my enlistment so I wouldn't have to -- I didn't want to come back right away. I wanted to see what -- hey, the war was over. I haven't done any fighting. But I wanted to see Europe. Here's my chance. See. And so I did. I stayed. And boy, I had a good time for the next year. It was fine, fabulous. Occupation duty was absolutely marvelous.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell us a little bit about what that was like.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Occupation duty was a cup of tea. Nobody did anything, really. I was not in the constabulary. I think they had it better than anyone. But I went to Bremerhaven and was in a replacement there where they was shipping people back to the United States and all that.. That was all I did was I called a roll every morning and then I was free. That was the end of it, and my day for a year. And then I get past this and went to Switzerland tours. I went to Italy. And oh, gosh, all over Europe. Austria. All of the Scandinavian countries, up to Bremen. Bremen was my favorite town in Germany out of all of them, up on the Weser River, north Germany, a very good place. If you ever get a chance go there, even now it's a good country. That's where you catch the ferry to Denmark and a very nice place to be.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What about the damage that had occurred in Germany?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: There was absolutely not a building standing that I saw anywhere in the country of Germany except a couple of cathedrals. Now, the housing was -- like Bremen,Germany, not one standing house. The only thing standing was concrete bunkers. There were a lot of those still that had not been wiped completely to rubble. But that was devastating. But of course, if you had lived through World War II and heard all the propaganda -- well, it wasn't all propaganda, by gosh. It was true. You didn't feel sorry for them. No. Hey, you were conquered. Hey, we won.That's your idea. Then you only got -- once you met some people that were halfway dear, just people like yourself, then you're -- your idea started changing; well, they may be Germans, but they're still -- they're still people. See. Before that, you only thought of them as the enemy. You did not think of them as humans at all. And if you did, you're not a good soldier. Good soldiers do not think in war about their opposition being human at all. They are numbers. That's it. Because otherwise, those numbers will blow your head off if you get to feeling too much sympathy. So you don't dare. See. That's the attitude. Now, once it was over, of course, and you met some people, then okay, let's rebui ld your country. It's okay. Hitler is not here anymore, blah, blah, blah.That was pretty much it. That's pretty much the attitude and actually a right one, I think. Maybe not.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What about the condition of the people, food?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: They had nothing. They were absolutely -- that was the sad part. When the war was over -- well, the first year was over, to give you an example, a carton of cigarettes in Berlin was worth $200 script not marks.American script. Well, now $200 for a carton of cigarettes is a lot of money. That was -- the underground economy was rampant, of course, in Europe. And whether you wanted to participate or not, if you -- if you wanted to go on a pass or whatever, the first thing you were asked, do you have any cigarettes. Well, if you didn't have any, you didn't get any -- you didn't do anything. Let's face it, because cigarettes were money in Europe, particularly in Germany. See.That was for the first year. And then during the second year they went down to 10, $15 a carton and because they were still And by that time people because the demand was less. the economy got better. How or why, I don't know, because I wasn't paying that much attention to the economy. But I do realize -- I did realize that that was the way it went. But for instance, if you were hungry and you were at the edge of town or whatever -- see, they -- the Germans don't live the way we do. No place in Europe does, really. Their farms were all outside of town. And the people did not live on the farms. They went out from the town to the farm and farmed it and then come back home.So you go out and you -- two cigarettes would buy you a dozen eggs at one time. That's just -- that's how expensive cigarettes were. They didn't smoke them. They just traded them. See. And they looked at Americans as though they were absolutely insane when they stand around smoking a cigarette worth $10. That struck me as kind of too lopsided. Now, that was mainly in the big towns, like Berlin and like that. Out in the countryside, no, they didn't -- no. The Germans, they were pretty organized. I enjoyed -- well, they thought -- I say I enjoyed. I appreciated it simply because I was not used to Americans being that organized in this country because we're not socialists. We are capitalists. And Germany, after the war, if you owned a pig, you didn't own that pig. That pig belonged to the community in which you lived, and it would be divided up amongst the people. I thought that was a good idea, because otherwise, there would have been people starve to death. So they shared everything. It was a communal thing in a way. Not necessarily the economy but whatever commodities they had, they had to share. There's no doubt about it. Some of them tried to hide. And of course, some did, no doubt. And like in Bremenhaven, these little towns and stuff, I met a lot of Germans that were farmers and so forth, and I had people offer me money to steal their pig. The government is going to take it and I won't ever they are not going to pay me enough and all this stuff. I said don't be greedy. Give somebody a pork chop, Willy. You know what I mean? I wouldn't help them. But that's the way it was.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Did you wind up seeing any of the concentration camps when you were there? W ILLIAM GRANT COLEMAN : Yeah, I saw one. And I didn't really want to see it. That's -- oh, God. That's sick. That's horrible. See, that's another reason that I was kind of hardened towards the Germans, why they -- they all said well, we didn't know that. Well, bologna, somebody had to know something. Right? You can't -- everything was not just Hitler's people and the Nazis. Whatever. Come on. I realize that they -- they were programmed and they were manipulated, the people that -- the common folk. But the Germans are very intelligent obviously. So I don't think -- I think they knew. Yeah. Yeah. They probably regret it, and they most certainly should. I thought it was horrible. I couldn't stand it.I -- I had seen some bad stuff in my days but nothing like that. No. No. We got prisoners of war back of our own that were in bad shape, too, actually. But nothing like the way they treated ethnic -- this ethnic thing. Agh, horrible. Horrible.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: I have heard also that there were a lot of displaced people from other countries running around Germany there the first little bit after the war. Did you see those guys?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: I saw a lot of them. Mainly from Poland and Czechoslovakia. Oh, yeah, there was a lot of misplaced people. And they had no papers. And they were in trouble actually. The Germans were not -- themselves, if they had papers, were not in that big of trouble, because, like I say, they shared. But if you were a displaced person that had no papers, you were -- man, you were in big trouble and that's all there was to it. Not only with the Poland side but with whatever system they had the disbursing of commodities of any kind. You were in trouble. So the American Army hired a lot of DPs, just to give them a place to sleep, eat, whatever. And they would do anything. We had Russians. We had a couple of Russians that they couldn't cook. They hired out as cooks, but hell, they couldn't cook. They couldn't do anything really, because they had been on communal farms and stuff. They didn't have they didn't know what the hell to do. Really, and it was too bad. I remember in the company that I was in for a while we had one guy there that they taught him he was not totally unintelligent at all. It's just that he was -- he didn't know how to do anything. Somebody taught him how to start these fire -- these stoves for in the kitchens and pump them up and all this stuff. God, he become almost indispensable. He not only worked for my company but any other company that had those worn out stoves. And just that sort of thing. But that's just a little incident, of course. But that's the way it was. And the DPs, whatever happened to them, I have no idea. Because one day I got -- they said well, you got 90 days to stay in the Army. You're hitting the ship tomorrow. Barn, barn, two days or whatever. And that was the end of it. I was gone. I processed out and I come home.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell us about coming home and how you decided to -- or why you decided to get out and then why did you decided to come back.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Well, when I got back, my folks had come to Oregon at that time. And I got discharged in Camp Kilmer, New Jersey. And I actually went back to McAlest er, Oklahoma where they had been, had just left from, and they were in Oregon. I had no intentions of coming to Oregon. I didn't know a thing about Oregon. I didn't even care. So I went to Wyoming and went and got a job in a coal mine and paid pretty -- paid good money. But then I got a letter from my mother saying that they were in dire straits financially. My dad -- my dad came here to work on the railroad. He was 51 years old. The railroad wouldn't hire anybody over 50. That was his - he didn't my dad was not a guy who read the fine print or looked at anything well, I'm in good shape, blah, blah, blah. No, he didn't know what rule books were. Or he didn't know nothing about that sort of thing. The way we live today would have been -- oh, if my dad had lived, he would have been crazy, because oh, God, he wouldn't have made it at all. And he couldn't make it then because he was not a man that -- oh, why are they making these fool rules for? I'm 51, but I don't care. I'm in good shape, blah, blah, blah. Well, that isn't the way it is, is it? So they were broke. They went broke when they came here. God knows how. I never did find out exactly what happened to whatever money they had when they sold their cattle and stuff in Oklahoma. But they didn't -- they were not wastrels. My family was very conservative and honest and that sort of thing and worked for a living. I don't know how I can really put it. They -- they were not highly-educated people. But they were not bums. I'll tell you that. And he couldn't get a job. So I had to quit the -- my coal mining job, which was paying at the time $14 a shift, which was pretty good. Then I came and worked for the railroad for a year. I didn't like to work for the railroad. It was I don't know why I didn't like it. It just wasn't my thing. So I went back in the Army in'49, never dreaming that {laughter} there would be any such thing as Korea. The war is over, you know. Well, much to my surprise...

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: How did you wind up in the 56th Amphibious Tractor Battalion?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Because I had a specialty. Somewhere along the line -- and it's a long story, I guess. Part of it had to do with the coal mining and so forth. I have an affinity for constructive destruction. I can cut a log in two with powder. I can pull a root out from under your driveway and not break the concrete. I know how to use powder. See. Explosives. And I don't know -- even know how I learned it, except just trial and error, whatever, in the mines and so forth and working. Well, that's what put me in the 56th Amphibious Tractor Battalion, because they were shock troops. 800 people that go where they're needed; get in, get out, rescue people, blow up something, do whatever. And that's what we did.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Hold on a minute while we change tapes out. {Pause} Tell us what the 56th was and tell us what your days were like before the war started.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Well, I was not there before the war started. I was only ther about -- let's see, the war started in June. And the 56th at that time was -- they were just being formed in Takayama, Japan, which is near Yokosuka, which is Seven Fleet headquarters on Tokyo Bay near Zushi and Kamakura and Yokahoma. Three -- Yokosuka, Zushi, Kamakura and Yokahoma was in a line up the beach from me. And Yokosuka is on a peninsula. Takayama is, too. That was where was an old Japanese camp had been. And they had barracks and that sort of thing, three-story jobby. But that was our headquarters from day one. It was formed and started there. And when I got to -- I had no idea that was what I would be going into when I got off the plane in Tokyo. And they flew me, incidentally, from Vancouver, Briti sh Columbia, Canadian Airway s, to Tokyo. Went to Camp Drake. And I thought my orders would be to go to Pusan, whatever. Because at that time Pusan was about all there was left actually in Korea when I got there. And the Koreans had already taken everything else. So they cut orders for me to report to Takayama to the 56th Amphibious Tank and Tractor. So I joined Dog Company as a tank driver. I had never been on a Mar k IV. I had no idea how to even start the thing or whatever. But that's why they gave it to me. Everyone -- then I found out in the 56th Amphibious Tank and Tractor had a minimum of 3MOSs. They specialized in three different things, at least three, and some of them more. See. I happened to have three MOSS, and one of them, of course, is demo. And why they put me as a driver, I haven't the slightest idea. I didn't even have a driver's license. But it didn't take me long to learn, of course. So we were trained a little bit. Then that was like sometime the last of August. And then in September we got on the LST and headed for Korea across the old yellow sand and went to Incheon. And before -- we stayed out to sea. They took us in at high tide. Well, at low tide they had taken pictures of all of the underwater obstruction in the Incheon Harbor, which at that time were made up of -- I'm trying to think of what they called them. There was three railroad rails in a triangle. And they are welded -- or bolted together at the top and just below the water line at high tide, and they would rip the bottom right out of a boat. So what we did, us and the Navy UDT, underwater demolition team, used primer cord and blew as many of these things up as we could find. And we found a bunch of them. And made channels, see, for the waves to go through an area at high tide the next day. And the next day we took over. But the Koreans were warned by the explosions in the harbor. Hey, they couldn't help but know it. The only problem was they weren't there and Korea and in Incheon itself we had very little opposition. We had some opposition in Kwajalein Island, which was in the harbor, and the Navy took care of that. They blasted the hell out of that. And then we went in. There was the First Marines Division and the Seventh Army Division and us. And we were with every wave that went in. Some of us were with every wave that went in, in to Incheon Harbor and through the beach. And then they organized and went -- and then it was about -- I'm trying to think. There was seven -- either five or seven lines of resistance supposedly on the military maps between Incheon and Seoul. And within two and a half days we were in Seoul. And a couple more days we were north of Seoul across the 38th and headed north. That was it. So there was very few casualties. We got none. Some of the Marines did, but I'm not sure it wasn't friendly fire, because boy, they liked to shoot. And just north of Seoul is where I met a lady that you guys have probably heard of, and she got killed in Vietnam. And probably of all the 50,000 -- 50,000-some people killed, that was the one I missed the most. And her name was Maggie Higgins. Sweetest woman in the world. She was a war correspondent. And she went up with us. She reported to Life magazine. And if you read about the Incheon Landing, Maggie wrote it. But she did not edit it. She was upset as hell, because according to Life magazine the only people that went in Incheon was Marines. Well, that's not true. There was a lot of Army went in. In fact, more than there was Marines. But of course that the Seventh Army Division don't make news but the Marines do. See. And this was true. We didn't care. My outfit, we -- I didn't care. All I wanted to do was get this thing over with, what are we doing, and get out of here. Because actually, I couldn't see -- well, I wasn't even nervous anymore, because we didn't get that much resistance. And when we did, it was easy. But what we didn't realize, we were passing by people that were just kind of laying low. And that's what happened to the Marines when they went north, all the way up through North Korea to Chosin Reservoir in November. But we pulled out. That's before they went up there, of course. They went past their main line of resistance is what they did and they got surrounded. And I can't really blame them, because that -- hey, there was not that much resistance. And they were taking the north Koreans without a problems. See. Which they should. They were trained for it. But we went back to Takayama and then we heard that there was -- the people that hung them needed to be helped out and evacuated. So that was just north of Pusan. So we want back and got them. That was my second skirmish in Korea. And that was a little bit more action. A lot more action actually. Until we lost a couple of people and several amphibs and one thing or another. There, getting those people out, there was a lot of them, but the North Koreans had no prisoners then. We got all of the prisoners out of there. That was what the evacuation was for. And a lot of civilians. American civilians actually. Then we went back -- now, all this is happening in the fall of'50, September through October. That's when we made the evacuation, in October. Then in November, the Marines, they got surrounded not all but part of the Marines got surrounded up on the Chosin Reservoir, which was the outer river between Manchurian and North Korea. And at 30 and 40 below zero, they were running out of ammo and everything else. And here is Chinese by the -- gee, I don't know how many Chinese. There was estimations. But -- and here, we are only had 800 people. This is where I was telling you that I got nominated for the -- this metal because -- and I think I didn't get it because nobody believed it, and I didn't -- I wasn' t the one that told them. Hey, I had no idea, because all I was doing was burning, burning cordite. Boy. So 800 of us wiped out two full Chinese divisions in 24 hours, and we only lost eight men. Not bad. Now, that shows you how crazy that those people were. They had no radios. They used trumpets. They were blowing horns. Some of them had guns. Some didn't. They were in -- some of them even had cotton pajamas or not pajamas but padded. It was cold. I don't know how in the hell they even moved. But we also knew that there was like -- see, there is such a thing as being absolutely swamped by numbers. Individually these people were not good soldiers. They were just meat. Hey, they were just masses. But they would overrun you. And that's -- thank God, we had enough ammo that we didn't get overrun and we got the Marines out. But that was Korea. See. Impossible to imagine how money people there was trying to -- that gave their lives for nothing, just because a damn bugle was blowing. See. It was ridiculous but very unnerving too, I might add. You think man, I only got so much ammo here. So we got the job done. Went back to -- and got out of there, of course. And got the Marines out. And that was -- that was when they started talking peace, which was -- they had us -- they've been talking peace ever since, and that was 50 years ago or better, over 50 years ago, and they are still talking it. And they still got the war going on. So it never did end. They could have ended that war right then, had -- now this is my personal opinion. Hey, I don't know. But I do believe if MacArthur had had his way, and he was a general not a politician, even though he's been accused of being one. And he was politically incorrect, that's for sure. But he would have ended that thing right there. And the domino effect, there wouldn't have been any Vietnam. There wouldn't have been any of that stuff because America would not have become a paper tiger. Because when we started talking instead of acting, to the Asian mind we were paper tigers. That's it. They paid no attention to us anymore. Yeah. That's right. And that started the whole domino thing. They started they was talking about the domino effect; well, if we do this or that, we'll lose this and we'll start World War III and all that. That was bologna. No, absolutely not.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So how about taking a minute and describing what the Amphib was like and

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The Mark IV?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: It was a -- kind of a morphodite piece of equipment. It looked like a tank. It had tracks like a tank. But it had pontoons built in the sides. And it was very lightly armored. The only armor was in front would have been about a half inch of steel, maybe three-quarters. I can't remember exactly. If you got a front of fire, right into the front from a rifle, small arm firearm, so forth, it would just ricochet off. But if you shot into the pontoons, you could sink it. See. It was very, very lightly armed as far as armor is concerned. But we had 75 Howitzers and we had twin 50s and I think -- oh, there was three 30s that could be mounted, because the radio man, assistant driver, gunner, and commander, that was -- in my case was me. Well, we all could have had a.30 caliber besides. We didn't have to use the 50s except under circumstances, different circumstances. And our -- and we had a gunner that fired a Frank 75 -- or not a Frank but 75 Howitzer, which acted like a mortar actually. The vehicle itself, now, that was -- that was -- I'm trying to think of the Mark IV. There was a III and a IV. The IV I believe was armored with with the turret, and the one without it was a III. I believe that's it. They carried ammo and troops. It was a landing craft. Both of them were. And they -- they used radio engine from seven -- some of them had seven, but most of them had 11 cylinder radio engines in them, which were very powerful engines and worked very well. They used very, very high octane fuel, though. Nothing less than a hundred. And -- oh, and the final drive was in front, of course, to pull the tracks, the front end drive. And you had, of course, your laterals and your clutches, the same way that a regular tank would have.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: And how did it move through the water?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: It moved through it -- you could get up to eight knots out of one under ideal circumstances and not less load. But it went four, five knots top speed. When you're going through the beach, the problem was with beach, if you had, say, a four to six, eight foot surf, it was fine. But when you had a beach, you are in high gear going through the water. High gear because you are getting no resistance and you're going as fast as you can. But when you hit this sand, or the beach, the thing stops because you have to use a clutch and put it in a lower gear. You have to stop it to put it in a lower gear, as a matter of fact. You could not double clutch one. That was a very fatal mistake on the engineering. Because if you had, say, a 10 to 12-foot surf and you stopped that thing, and it hit the ass end of it, you flipped over. That's it. And you drowned your crew, because hey -- and that's -- we lost people that -- it hung them, that way, eight or ten of them we lost, because of -- not because of enemy fire but because we swamped the vehicles because they had a 12-foot surf. Yeah. Not -- it's not -- not a reliable vehicle at all. And on land, which they were -- we had to use them on land, those grousers that, you know, they cut the water on the tracks, the tracks were light and they were bolted on. Double circle like this {indicating}, and they were about three and a half inches high, and one right after the other going around. Well, sure, they would blow the water. They would take off. But on land, too flimsy. Hey, you hit a rock or something, you knock one off. So they really wasn't worth much off the beach.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Must have been a little exciting to fire the gun when you're in the water.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: To Fire the 75-millimeter gun when you're in the water must have got your attention.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: {Laughter} It was. See. Yeah. But you get used to all of that stuff. See. Yeah. Yeah. It becomes even though it's very dangerous and very crazy, it becomes mundane after a while. It's like well, the first time is kinky and the next time is habit. You know what I mean?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: That's the way it is. You get used to practically anything, which sometimes gets you hurt. A lot of times. Most of the time it does actually. The training was every day. I spent three years in that outfit and I - I enjoyed every day of it. Actually I enjoyed the excitement of it. It was a good outfit. It really was. Mainly because it was small. You knew every -- I knew every single person in that outfit. See. It doesn't take you forever to learn 800 people. And there wasn't that much -- there wasn't that much turnover because we didn't really lose that many men. See. Attrition did not take that many people. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Now, the second or third day on the beach at Incheon, the North Koreans sent some t34 tanks in there, and you guys got involved in a firefight with them? What was that like?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: That wasn't that -- it wasn't as bad as you think, because the North Koreans -- the funny thing is the t34 was a heck of a tank. It was a good tank. But they had some very poorly trained people running those tanks obviously. See. I don't have this picture with me, but I have it at home. I think probably the most anger that I felt in Korea was during this time. I looked through my glasses and I saw -- well, actually through a site, which was about 15 power, and saw a Shell Oil Company truck refueling a t34 tank and I couldn't believe my eyes. That's when I told Linker, my driver, I said take a look. He took a look. He said come on. He said that's Ameri ca. I said well, of course, we didn't realize then that Shell Oil Company belonged to Holland and they would sell to anybody on Earth, anybody that would buy gas. They didn't care. We didn't know that. We just thought all Shell stations were American. See. I said what are you going to do about that, Linker. He said tell the gunner that -- show it to the gunner. So I showed it to Josh. He said what do you want me to do, George. I said I want you to blow that sucker up. Well, he said yeah, but there might be Americans there. I said I don't care. They are filling a t34 and we don't have any t34s. Blow it up. Boom. We did. And see, I couldn't tell anybody else because we had radio silence. After that sucker went off, and man, it made a hell of a noise and fire -- oh, God, you can imagine an oil a gasoline tanker blowing. Boy, I had a lieutenant come up and he was screaming what did you think you're doing, blah, blah, you've given our position away. I said it doesn't matter. The guy is gone, long gone. He said yeah, but he said wasn't that -- wasn't he filling wasn't that American. I said no. He said well, it's Shell Oil. I said I don't care. It's a t34. I took him out. Come to find out that none of us -- how naive could we be. Hey, Shell is an international company. They can sell to anybody they want to, and they were selling gasoline to the north Koreans. Russia. To anybody else that would buy it, just like Krupp would sell to Germany. You know what I mean? Same thing. So that's when I started to lose my innocence a great deal, see, and become just a little bit more aware that all isn't right here. Something is really stupid going on. And then after they fired MacArthur, the only general that I knew of that I was under that knew up from sideways, that wasn't a politician, and he had really straightened out the Japanese, there is no doubt about that, he done a good job. But he was too big for his britches. See. How stupid can you get? We found out since, my little insight was right. And I don't like to brag about it, because I have no way of -- I couldn't tell you in a million years why I thought this way, but I knew something was wrong. You take some idiot that got elected that was nothing but a captain in World War I telling a general, who is a genius, that he's too big for his britches. That didn't make sense to me. And it still don't. And it never will. Bologna. Bologna. No.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So other than removing the landing obstacles at Incheon, did you do any demolition work while you were there?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Not while I was there, no. There really wasn't much. The Navy had taken care of most of that, the UDT did. The problem is that, see, Incheon is -- has gone down in history as a hell of a battle. It wasn't a hell of a battle. It was a very good strategy. It wasn't even a good skirmish. I'm telling you. Take my word for it, the Battle of Incheon wasn't a battle. We got no resistance. They didn't even know we -- that was the last place in the world they thought they would be invaded, because it was miles from land. At low tide you could see for miles mudflats. And they thought hey, no ships American ships are going to come in here. They are not too stupid. Well, they didn't. They weren't that stupid either. We blew out channels for them to come in. That was it. See. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Now let's talk about whatever it was that you picked up that --

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Well, I don't know when -- I know -- I think I know when I got this. It was when we were in North Korea up in northern -- up near the Yalu on that part icular action, we run out of water. They didn't -- hey, we were supposed to go in and out. Well, it was three or four days before we could get out. So we had no halazone tablets, and neither did the Marines, purification tablets for our water, whatever we use. So we melted snow. All right. That didn't mean we boiled it. We just melted it. And I think that is where I picked up this -- my immune system could not do something with whatever was in this snow. It wasn't yellow snow. It was fresh snow. But nevertheless, you breathe the air in the San Joaquin Valley, if you weren't born there, you're like a -- it's like a baby playing with a cat. Hey, it goes blind. Same thing. Toxoplasmosis. I have no idea what it is. Yep. And that's where I got it. And the reason that they know it's where I got it was because it was several more people got it, and there weren't that many of us to begin with, you see, there. And so they pinpointed it there. Since then, of course, and not very long after that, the medical science had known of this disease before in Korea. And so they -- they put two and two together. And that was our diagnosis. And they were absolutely right. I obviously went blind. And there was not a damn thing I could do to stop it. I was through. So there I am. Here I am. Yep.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, now, this is probably going to be kind of a silly question. But how do you feel about that? Your time in the military cost you your sight, ultimately when you get right down to it. So how do you feel about that?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Well, I can't be bitter. I'll tell you why. Simply because I was just at the wrong place at the right -- the wrong time. As far as my -- any action in the military that I took, I don't regret one bit of it or going there at all. There's people coming back here in a lot worst shape than me, first of all, and that's not been brought out or anything else. The only thing that bugs me and it makes me bitter is the fact that the whole thing was useless. They are still fighting the damn war, and this was 52 years ago or 54 years ago. Why? See. It just -- see, what bugs me is not losing my sight but uselessly. You see, it was so useless. Totally useless. The whole thing was useless. Gosh. Now, that does irritate me. It really does. Not losing my sight. I could have lost my sight out here playing baseball or whatever. Anybody can. That wasn't it. See.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Okay. Well, now you also mentioned that you wound up in Vietnam. Do you want to just tell us how that happened?

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: Well, when we went back when I went back I was -- I trained people. You know, we were trained constantly actually. We went to Okinawa. We went all over. I did not go to Vietnam to train people. I had -- hate to tell you this, because it sounds like I was goofing off, and I was. I had a job as an instructor, two hours a day and that's -- that was it. My day was over after two hours instruction. The Marines didn't want us training them anyway. So it was very, very easy to goof off. We would have a class and, you know, whatever. So what I would do two days a week I would give somebody a couple thousand yen to take my place. That's two days. And then I would do talk to the Marine lieutenant and he would say well, we don't -- we want to do so and so and so forth for another two days. So there is four days. If that started on Monday, that gave me from Friday until -- it gave me a week off. I had nothing to do. See. I could take off. So I did. And I got -- I got to go over on to this hangout at the airbase that had a good bar over there and buzzing with ponsk ies (phonetic) and people soliciting there all the damn time and everything. I got to talking to these guys, these military air transport pilots and got acquainted with several of them. Finally this one guy said why don't you go with me, we would only be gone three days. Would you like to see a beautiful place. I will drop my cargo and we'll go on down to Saigon. He said now there's a town you can have fun in. Well, it was kind of hard to turn down, so I went to Saigon about four or five times in 1952. Yeah. That's -- and now I think about it, how lucky can you get. I went to Vietnam just to have fun. That's true. I had a ball. I enjoyed it very much. But to go there as a fighter, no, absolutely did not. And didn't want to either. No. Because just flying over where those people -- like I told you before, the jungle frightens me more than people do. I don't like it.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: All right. That's great. That's the end of the tape. And I think we covered it all pretty well.

sp.speaker: William Grant Coleman
sp.p: That's about the end of my story.
